identification.summary: Microsoft tracks Pepper Typhoon as a China-origin actor and maps it to CrowdStrike's LIMINAL PANDA and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42's CL-STA-0969 [S1]. CrowdStrike describes LIMINAL PANDA as an actor that has targeted telecommunications entities since at least 2020, using custom tools for covert access, command and control (C2) and data exfiltration [S2][S4]. The actor uses telecom-specific protocols (GSM, SIGTRAN) and has used compromised telecom servers to start intrusions into further providers in other regions [S2][S4]. Unit 42 reported a February-November 2024 campaign by CL-STA-0969 against telecom operators, which it says heavily overlaps with Liminal Panda [S6][S7][S8].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike: active since at least 2020 [S2][S4]. CrowdStrike says some activity it now attributes to LIMINAL PANDA was earlier attributed to LightBasin [S2][S3]. First public naming as LIMINAL PANDA: 2024-11-19 [S2][S5].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Pepper Typhoon, origin China, other names LIMINAL PANDA and CL-STA-0969 [S1]. Microsoft has published no Pepper Typhoon reporting in the sources gathered, so the substance of this profile comes from CrowdStrike (LIMINAL PANDA) and Unit 42 (CL-STA-0969) [S2][S6]. Cluster boundaries differ: CrowdStrike split LIMINAL PANDA out of activity it had earlier called LightBasin, and Unit 42 reports tooling overlaps between CL-STA-0969 and LightBasin, UNC3886, UNC2891 and UNC1945 without merging those clusters [S2][S7]. Axios reports CrowdStrike saw no evidence of coordination between LIMINAL PANDA and Salt Typhoon [S5].

attribution.sponsor: China nexus (vendor assessment, not government attribution). Microsoft lists the origin of Pepper Typhoon as China [S1].
attribution.confidence: CrowdStrike assesses with low confidence that LIMINAL PANDA activity aligns with China-nexus cyber operations [S4]. CrowdStrike assesses with high confidence that the activity supports intelligence collection, based on target profile, likely mission objectives and observed TTPs [S2]. Unit 42 assesses with high confidence that CL-STA-0969 has a nation-state nexus and says the cluster heavily overlaps with Liminal Panda based on activity and victimology [S6][S7]. CrowdStrike linked the SIGweaver tool to LIMINAL PANDA with moderate confidence [S9]. No US government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike incident-response and intelligence reporting [S2][S3][S4]; Unit 42 incident reporting on CL-STA-0969 [S6][S7][S8]; Microsoft's alias mapping [S1]; Singapore IMDA advisory relaying CrowdStrike's SIGweaver reporting [S9].

objectives: Signals-intelligence-style collection from mobile networks, such as subscriber information, call metadata and device location, rather than financial gain [S2][S4][S6]. Unit 42 notes that use of Cordscan suggests that collecting victim location data was a likely objective [S6][S8].

sectors: Telecommunications (mobile network operators and GPRS/roaming providers) [S2][S6]
Telecom core network elements such as HSS, VLR, SGSN and NMS (SIGweaver reporting) [S9]
regions: Southeast Asia or Southwest Asia (Unit 42 CL-STA-0969; sources differ on wording) [S6][S8]
targeting.notes: CrowdStrike reports that the actor used compromised telecom servers to start intrusions into providers in other regions, so targeting can spread through inter-operator trust relationships [S2]. Unit 42 says the actors abused interconnected mobile roaming networks [S6]. Unit 42's executive summary says Southwest Asia, while Security Affairs coverage says Southeast Asia [S6][S8].

capabilities.summary: Telecom-specialist tradecraft. CrowdStrike reports public tools (TinyShell, ProxyChains), custom telecom tools (CordScan, SIGTRANslator), and use of mobile protocols such as GSM for C2 [S4]. Unit 42 reports likely initial access through SSH brute-forcing with credential lists built for telecom equipment [S8]. Its custom implants include AuthDoor (a malicious PAM module that captures credentials and allows access with a hard-coded password), GTPDoor (malware for hosts next to GPRS roaming exchanges), EchoBackdoor, ChronosRAT and NoDepDNS, plus a Serving GPRS Support Node emulator [S7][S8]. In January 2026, CrowdStrike linked SIGweaver to LIMINAL PANDA with moderate confidence. SIGweaver is a Linux kernel-level driver that injects malicious messages into live telecom traffic over SS7 (2G/3G) and Diameter (4G LTE) without opening new network connections. IMDA calls it the actor's first confirmed capability to operate natively in 4G infrastructure [S9].

campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reports multiple incidents against telecom operators, with access likely gained by SSH brute-force, deployment of AuthDoor, GTPDoor and other implants, and Cordscan used to try to collect device location. Unit 42 found no clear evidence of exfiltration.

campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike published LIMINAL PANDA reporting, and Axios covered it as a new China-linked group attacking telecom networks, separate from Salt Typhoon.

campaigns.name: SIGweaver 4G-capable implant
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike reporting, relayed by Singapore's IMDA, links the SIGweaver kernel driver for SS7/Diameter traffic injection to LIMINAL PANDA with moderate confidence.

diamond.adversary: Pepper Typhoon / LIMINAL PANDA / CL-STA-0969. CrowdStrike assesses with low confidence that it is China-nexus, and Unit 42 assesses with high confidence that it has a nation-state nexus [S1][S4][S6].
diamond.capability: Telecom-specific tools (CordScan, SIGTRANslator, SIGweaver), Linux implants (AuthDoor PAM backdoor, GTPDoor, EchoBackdoor, ChronosRAT, NoDepDNS), and public tools (TinyShell, ProxyChains) [S4][S7][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised telecom servers used to pivot to other providers; GSM, GTP, DNS, ICMP and SSH channels for C2 [S2][S4][S7].
diamond.victim: Mobile network operators and their core and roaming elements (HSS, VLR, SGSN, NMS, GPRS roaming exchanges) in South Asia, Africa and Southeast/Southwest Asia [S6][S7][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on mobile subscribers, call metadata and device location, consistent with SIGINT goals rather than profit [S2][S4][S6].
diamond.technology: Trust between operators in roaming networks, legacy SS7/SIGTRAN and GTP signaling, Diameter in 4G, and internet-exposed Linux and telecom management hosts reachable by SSH [S6][S8][S9].

gaps: Microsoft has published no Pepper Typhoon reporting in the sources gathered; the Microsoft name comes only from the alias mapping [S1].

Primary documents could not be opened (fetch blocked): CrowdStrike blogs [S2][S3], the Unit 42 report [S6] and the IMDA advisories [S9]. Facts are drawn from search excerpts and secondary coverage, and confidence wording should be checked against the originals.

Unclear confidence wording: coverage says CrowdStrike's China-nexus assessment is low confidence and its intelligence-collection assessment is high confidence. Confirm the exact statements in the CrowdStrike blog.
Region discrepancy for CL-STA-0969: Unit 42 says Southwest Asia, while coverage says Southeast Asia [S6][S8].
Not verified: a claim in secondary coverage that targets cluster in Belt and Road Initiative countries, and a claim that the 2024 disclosure came in US Senate testimony. Neither is included as fact.
Boundaries between LIMINAL PANDA, LightBasin (UNC1945), UNC2891 and UNC3886 are unresolved across vendors. Tooling overlaps do not prove a single operator [S2][S7].
No specific victims, sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA or contractor), or confirmed exfiltration volumes are public in the sources gathered.
Whether SIGweaver has been seen deployed in live victim networks, rather than only analyzed, is unclear [S9].
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry was identified for this actor.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key cyber terrain is commercial mobile-network core and roaming infrastructure (HSS, VLR, SGSN, GPRS roaming exchanges, signaling gateways) that carries location and metadata for deployed personnel and partner-nation officials using host-nation carriers [S6][S9]. STEP 2 (effects): Because operators trust each other on roaming links, a compromise in one partner-nation carrier can expose traffic from another, so collection risk reaches beyond the directly compromised carrier [S2][S6]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Access through SSH brute force or a compromised peer operator, then PAM backdoors and GTP/DNS/ICMP covert channels, then telecom-protocol tools (CordScan, SIGTRANslator, SIGweaver) for subscriber, metadata and location collection [S4][S7][S8][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent, low-noise collection of subscriber location and call metadata from carriers in South Asia, Africa and Southeast/Southwest Asia [S2][S6]. MDCOA is use of 4G-capable signaling injection (SIGweaver) during a crisis for location tracking, denial of service against subscribers, or covert C2 inside partner carriers that support US forces [S9]. Candidate indicators: unexpected PAM modules or changes on telecom Linux hosts; brute-force SSH against carrier management interfaces; anomalous GTP or DNS traffic near GPRS roaming exchanges; unsolicited SS7/Diameter location queries; unknown kernel modules on signaling nodes [S7][S8][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: telecom carriers in host and partner nations are outside the DODIN, so visibility depends on partner and vendor reporting; track carrier advisories (for example IMDA) and vendor reporting on this cluster [S6][S9]. (2) Authorities: defending a foreign commercial carrier is not a DoD action by default; any hunt-forward or partner support requires host-nation consent and coordination through the appropriate CCMD and interagency channels. (3) Mission assurance: assume mobile metadata and location on commercial networks in affected regions may be collected; enforce COMSEC and emissions discipline and prefer DoD-controlled transport for C2 [S2][S6]. (4) Coordination: fuse CrowdStrike, Unit 42 and Microsoft naming (LIMINAL PANDA / CL-STA-0969 / Pepper Typhoon) in common operational picture products, and keep LightBasin/UNC-cluster overlaps flagged as unresolved, to avoid double-counting or false merging [S1][S7].

provenance.importedSummary: LIMINAL PANDA is a China-nexus APT that targets telecommunications entities, employing custom malware and publicly available tools for covert access, C2, and data exfiltration. The adversary demonstrates extensive knowledge of telecom networks, utilizing GSM protocols to retrieve mobile subscriber information and call metadata. LIMINAL PANDA exploits trust relationships and security gaps between providers to access core infrastructure, indicating a focus on SIGINT collection rather than financial gain. Their intrusion activity has primarily affected telecom providers in southern Asia and Africa, with potential for broader targeting based on network configurations.
